en.faqQ1: What is the easiest language to learn for English speakers?
en.faqA1: For native English speakers, the easiest languages are typically in the Germanic and Romance families. Dutch, Norwegian, Swedish, and Afrikaans share the most vocabulary and grammar with English. Spanish, Portuguese, French, and Italian are also relatively easy due to their large shared Latin vocabulary. MyNextLanguage scores all 96 languages across lexical similarity, grammar distance, phonology, and writing system to give you a personalised ranking.
en.faqQ2: How long does it take to learn a new language?
en.faqA2: The Foreign Service Institute (FSI) groups languages into four tiers for English speakers. Category I (Spanish, French, Dutch) takes roughly 600–750 hours. Category II (German, Indonesian) takes about 900 hours. Category III (Russian, Hebrew, Thai) takes around 1,100 hours. Category IV (Arabic, Chinese, Japanese, Korean) takes approximately 2,200 hours.
en.faqQ3: How does MyNextLanguage calculate language difficulty?
en.faqA3: MyNextLanguage scores each language across five weighted dimensions: lexical similarity (shared vocabulary), grammatical distance (morphology and syntax), phonological similarity (shared sounds), writing system difficulty, and genealogical distance (language family position). You can adjust the dimension weights with the sliders.
en.faqQ4: Which language should I learn after Spanish?
en.faqA4: After Spanish, the closest languages are Portuguese, Italian, Catalan, Romanian, and French — all Romance languages with a large shared Latin vocabulary. Portuguese is often the easiest step from Spanish due to near-identical grammar and ~89% lexical overlap.
en.faqQ5: What languages are most similar to each other?
en.faqA5: The most mutually intelligible pairs include Serbian/Croatian, Norwegian/Swedish, Spanish/Portuguese, Czech/Slovak, and Malay/Indonesian. Use comparison mode to place any two languages side-by-side.

de.faqQ1: Welche Sprache ist für Deutschsprachige am leichtesten zu lernen?
de.faqA1: Für Deutschsprachige sind die leichtesten Sprachen typischerweise in der germanischen Familie: Niederländisch, Afrikaans, Schwedisch, Dänisch und Norwegisch teilen viel Wortschatz und Grammatik mit Deutsch. Auch Jiddisch und Luxemburgisch sind sehr nah.
de.faqQ2: Wie lange dauert es, eine neue Sprache zu lernen?
de.faqA2: Das FSI teilt Sprachen für Englischsprecher in vier Kategorien ein. Kategorie I (~600–750 Stunden): Spanisch, Französisch, Holländisch. Kategorie II (~900 Stunden): Deutsch, Indonesisch. Kategorie III (~1.100 Stunden): Russisch, Hebräisch. Kategorie IV (~2.200 Stunden): Arabisch, Chinesisch, Japanisch, Koreanisch.

de.faqQ4: Welche Sprache sollte ich nach Deutsch lernen?
de.faqA4: Nach Deutsch sind die nächsten Sprachen Niederländisch, Afrikaans, Schwedisch, Dänisch und Norwegisch — alle germanischen Sprachen mit engem grammatikalischen und lexikalischem Bezug.
de.faqQ5: Welche Sprachen sind sich am ähnlichsten?
de.faqA5: Die am stärksten gegenseitig verständlichen Paare sind Serbisch/Kroatisch, Norwegisch/Schwedisch, Spanisch/Portugiesisch, Tschechisch/Slowakisch und Malaiisch/Indonesisch.

fr.faqQ1: Quelle est la langue la plus facile à apprendre pour les francophones ?
fr.faqA1: Pour les francophones, les langues les plus faciles sont généralement dans la famille romane : l'espagnol, l'italien, le portugais, le catalan et le roumain partagent une grande partie du vocabulaire et de la grammaire avec le français.
fr.faqQ2: Combien de temps faut-il pour apprendre une nouvelle langue ?
fr.faqA2: Le FSI classe les langues en quatre catégories. Catégorie I (~600–750 heures) : espagnol, italien, portugais. Catégorie II (~900 heures) : allemand. Catégorie III (~1 100 heures) : russe, arabe. Catégorie IV (~2 200 heures) : chinois, japonais, arabe, coréen.

fr.faqQ4: Quelle langue apprendre après le français ?
fr.faqA4: Après le français, les langues les plus proches sont l'espagnol, l'italien, le portugais, le catalan et le roumain — toutes des langues romanes avec un large vocabulaire latin commun.
fr.faqQ5: Quelles langues se ressemblent le plus ?
fr.faqA5: Les paires les plus intelligibles mutuellement incluent serbe/croate, norvégien/suédois, espagnol/portugais, tchèque/slovaque et malais/indonésien.

pl.faqQ1: Jaki język jest najłatwiejszy do nauki dla Polaków?
pl.faqA1: Dla Polaków, najłatwiejsze języki to zazwyczaj inne języki słowiańskie: czeski, słowacki, ukraiński i rosyjski dzielą wiele gramatyki i słownictwa z polskim.
pl.faqQ2: Ile czasu zajmuje nauka nowego języka?
pl.faqA2: FSI dzieli języki na cztery kategorie. Kategoria I (~600–750 godzin): hiszpański, włoski, francuski. Kategoria II (~900 godzin): niemiecki. Kategoria III (~1100 godzin): rosyjski, hebrajski. Kategoria IV (~2200 godzin): arabski, chiński, japoński, koreański.
pl.faqA3: MyNextLanguage ocenia każdy język w pięciu wymiarach: podobieństwo leksykalne, dystans gramatyczny, podobieństwo fonologiczne, trudność systemu pisma i dystans genealogiczny.
pl.faqQ4: Jakiego języka uczyć się po polskim?
pl.faqA4: Po polskim, najbliższe języki to czeski, słowacki, ukraiński, rosyjski i białoruski — wszystkie słowiańskie z bliską gramatyką i słownictwem.
pl.faqQ5: Jakie języki są do siebie najbardziej podobne?
pl.faqA5: Najbardziej wzajemnie zrozumiałe pary to serbski/chorwacki, norweski/szwedzki, hiszpański/portugalski, czeski/słowacki i malajski/indonezyjski.
pl.faqA6: Tak — całkowicie bezpłatny, bez reklam, działa w przeglądarce bez konta ani instalacji. Obejmuje 96 języków świata i działa offline jako PWA.

tr.faqQ1: Türkçe bilenler için en kolay öğrenilecek dil nedir?
tr.faqA1: Türkçe bilenler için en kolay diller genellikle Türk dil ailesindeki dillerdir: Azerbaycan dili, Özbekçe, Kazakça ve Kırgızca Türkçe ile büyük gramatik ve sözcüksel benzerlik paylaşır.
tr.faqQ2: Yeni bir dil öğrenmek ne kadar sürer?
tr.faqA2: FSI, dilleri İngilizce konuşanlar için dört kategoriye ayırır. Kategori I (~600–750 saat): İspanyolca, Fransızca. Kategori II (~900 saat): Almanca. Kategori III (~1.100 saat): Rusça, Türkçe. Kategori IV (~2.200 saat): Arapça, Çince, Japonca, Korece.
tr.faqA3: MyNextLanguage her dili beş boyutta değerlendirir: sözcüksel benzerlik, dilbilgisel mesafe, sesbilimsel benzerlik, yazı sistemi zorluğu ve soysal mesafe.
tr.faqA4: Türkçeden sonra en yakın diller Azerbaycan dili, Özbekçe, Kazakça, Kırgızca ve Türkmencedir — hepsi aynı dil ailesinden.
tr.faqQ5: Hangi diller birbirine en çok benziyor?
tr.faqA5: En yüksek karşılıklı anlaşılabilirlik çiftleri: Sırpça/Hırvatça, Norveççe/İsveççe, İspanyolca/Portekizce, Çekçe/Slovakça ve Malayca/Endonezce.
tr.faqA6: Evet — tamamen ücretsiz, reklamsız ve hesap ya da kurulum gerektirmeden tarayıcınızda çalışır. 96 dünya dilini kapsar ve PWA olarak çevrimdışı çalışır.

ru.faqQ1: Какой язык легче всего выучить носителям русского?
ru.faqA1: Для носителей русского языка, самые лёгкие языки — как правило, другие славянские: украинский, белорусский, болгарский, польский, чешский и словацкий имеют много общего с русским в плане грамматики и лексики.
ru.faqQ2: Сколько времени нужно для изучения нового языка?
ru.faqA2: FSI делит языки на четыре категории. Категория I (~600–750 часов): испанский, французский, итальянский. Категория II (~900 часов): немецкий. Категория III (~1100 часов): русский, иврит. Категория IV (~2200 часов): арабский, китайский, японский, корейский.
ru.faqA3: MyNextLanguage оценивает каждый язык по пяти измерениям: лексическое сходство, грамматическое расстояние, фонологическое сходство, сложность письменности и генеалогическое расстояние.
ru.faqA4: После русского, ближайшие языки — украинский, белорусский, болгарский, польский и сербский/хорватский — все славянские с близкой грамматикой и лексикой.
ru.faqQ5: Какие языки наиболее похожи друг на друга?
ru.faqA5: Наиболее взаимопонятные пары: сербский/хорватский, норвежский/шведский, испанский/португальский, чешский/словацкий и малайский/индонезийский.
ru.faqA6: Да — совершенно бесплатно, без рекламы, работает в браузере без учётной записи или установки. Охватывает 96 мировых языков и работает офлайн как PWA.

af.description: A West Germanic language that evolved from 17th-century Dutch, spoken natively by around 7 million people primarily in South Africa and Namibia. Its simplified grammar (no verb conjugation for person, no grammatical gender) makes it one of the most accessible Germanic languages for English speakers.

am.description: The official working language of Ethiopia and the second-most widely spoken Semitic language in the world, with around 22 million native speakers. It uses the distinctive Ethiopic (Ge'ez) script and is notable for its ejective consonants and complex verb morphology.

ar.description: Modern Standard Arabic is the formal written form used across 22 Arab nations in media, literature, and government, and as the liturgical language of Islam it is understood by hundreds of millions worldwide. As one of the six official languages of the United Nations, fluency opens doors across the Middle East, North Africa, and Muslim-majority communities globally.

az.description: A Turkic language spoken natively by around 30 million people across Azerbaijan, northwestern Iran, and diaspora communities. Closely related to Turkish, it underwent a dramatic script shift — Arabic to Cyrillic to Latin — following Azerbaijani independence in 1991.

be.description: An East Slavic language closely related to Russian and Ukrainian, spoken natively by around 6–7 million people in Belarus, though Russian dominates urban daily life. Its distinctive soft consonants and vocabulary set it apart from its Slavic neighbors, and it has seen renewed cultural interest since 2020.

bg.description: A South Slavic language notable for being the first Slavic language to be written down (in Old Church Slavonic) and for several unusual features within its family: it has definite articles and largely lacks grammatical cases for nouns. Spoken by around 8 million people in Bulgaria, it uses the Cyrillic alphabet.

bn.description: An Indo-Aryan language spoken natively by around 234 million people, making it the fifth-most spoken language in the world by native speakers. The official language of Bangladesh and the state language of West Bengal, it has a rich literary tradition crowned by Nobel laureate Rabindranath Tagore.

bo.description: A Sino-Tibetan language spoken natively by around 6 million Tibetans across the Tibetan Plateau, Bhutan, Nepal, and India. Written in the elegant Tibetan script introduced in the 7th century, it has an extraordinarily rich tradition of Buddhist philosophical and scientific texts that have been translated from Sanskrit.

ca.description: A vibrant Romance language with around 9–10 million speakers across Catalonia, Valencia, the Balearic Islands, Andorra (where it's the sole official language), and pockets of France and Italy. Despite lacking its own sovereign state, Catalan has a rich medieval literary tradition and is co-official in several Spanish autonomous communities.

cs.description: A West Slavic language spoken by around 10.7 million people in the Czech Republic, known for its rich literary tradition and notably complex phonology — including the rare consonantal syllable, as in the tongue-twister 'strč prst skrz krk'. Its 7-case system and 3-gender grammar typify West Slavic structure.

cy.description: A Brittonic Celtic language spoken natively by around 870,000 people in Wales, UK — one of the most successful language revitalization stories in Europe. Supported by government policy, Welsh-medium education, and the S4C television channel, it's notable for its initial consonant mutations and for being the only Celtic language to have grown its speaker base in recent decades.

da.description: A North Germanic language and the official language of Denmark, spoken by around 6 million people and mutually intelligible with Norwegian and partly with Swedish. Its distinctive 'stød' (a glottal constriction feature) and swallowed consonants give Danish its characteristic melodic sound.

de.description: A West Germanic language spoken natively by around 76 million people — the most widely spoken native language in the European Union. Known for its compound words ('Donaudampfschifffahrtsgesellschaft'), three grammatical genders, four-case system, and rich literary tradition spanning Goethe, Schiller, and Kafka.

el.description: One of the world's oldest recorded languages, with an unbroken literary tradition spanning over 3,400 years from Homer to the present day. Spoken natively by around 13.5 million people in Greece and Cyprus, Classical Greek forms the etymological backbone of much of the world's scientific, philosophical, and medical vocabulary.

en.description: The world's primary global lingua franca, with around 400 million native speakers and 1.5 billion total speakers across every continent. Shaped by Germanic roots, Norman French, and Latin, English has become the de facto language of science, technology, aviation, diplomacy, and international business.

es.description: A Romance language with around 485 million native speakers — the world's second most widely spoken native language — and official status across 20 countries spanning Europe, Latin America, Africa, and the United States. Spanish is the dominant language of the Western Hemisphere and a pillar of global culture, from literature to music to cinema.

et.description: A Finno-Ugric language closely related to Finnish, spoken natively by around 1.1 million people in Estonia — one of the world's most digitally advanced nations. Its 14 grammatical cases, long compound words, and complete unrelatedness to neighboring Indo-European languages make it a fascinating challenge.

eu.description: One of Europe's greatest linguistic mysteries — a language isolate with no known relatives anywhere on Earth, spoken by around 750,000 people in the Basque Country straddling northern Spain and southwestern France. Its agglutinative grammar, ancient vocabulary, and ergative-absolutive case system place it entirely outside the Indo-European family.

fa.description: An Iranian language with an unbroken literary tradition spanning over 2,500 years — the language of Rumi, Hafez, and Omar Khayyam — and the official language of Iran, Afghanistan (as Dari), and Tajikistan (as Tajik). Spoken natively by around 70–110 million people, it was once the administrative and cultural lingua franca from Anatolia to Bengal.

fi.description: A Finno-Ugric language entirely unrelated to its Indo-European neighbors, spoken by around 5.4 million people in Finland and minority communities in Sweden and Norway. Famous for its 15 grammatical cases, vowel harmony, extremely long compound words, and agglutinative morphology.

fo.description: A North Germanic language spoken by around 66,000 people in the Faroe Islands, directly descended from the Old Norse brought by Viking settlers. Despite its tiny speaker population it boasts a thriving modern literature, its own Wikipedia, and high mutual intelligibility with Icelandic.

fr.description: A Romance language spoken natively by around 80 million people and as an official language across 29 countries on five continents, making it one of the most geographically widespread languages in the world. As a language of diplomacy, cuisine, fashion, and literature, French carries immense cultural prestige and opens doors across Europe, Africa, and the Americas.

ga.description: A Goidelic Celtic language and the first official language of Ireland, though spoken natively in Gaeltacht areas by only around 100,000–170,000 people today. Known for its VSO word order (verb-subject-object), initial consonant mutations, and lenition, it's a living link to the pre-Roman Celtic world.

gl.description: A Romance language spoken by around 2.4 million people in Galicia, the northwestern corner of Spain, sitting linguistically between Spanish and Portuguese. So closely related to Portuguese that many linguists historically grouped them as one 'Galician-Portuguese' language — mutual comprehension is very high.

gn.description: A Tupian language co-official with Spanish in Paraguay, where it is spoken by around 90% of the population — making it the most widely spoken indigenous language in the Americas with genuine national official status. Around 6–7 million people speak it, often in a natural mixed form with Spanish called Jopará.

gu.description: An Indo-Aryan language spoken natively by around 56 million people, primarily in the Indian state of Gujarat, with a highly mobile diaspora in the UK, USA, and East Africa. Written in its own Gujarati script (descended from Devanagari), it's the language of Mahatma Gandhi and a major language of Indian commerce.

ha.description: A Chadic language of the Afro-Asiatic family, serving as the most important trade lingua franca across West Africa with 60–80 million native speakers and many more L2 users across Nigeria, Niger, Ghana, and Cameroon. It uses a modified Latin alphabet (Boko) in modern contexts but has a centuries-long tradition of Arabic-script literacy.

he.description: One of history's most remarkable linguistic revival stories — a Semitic language restored as a living spoken tongue in the 19th–20th century after nearly two millennia of use primarily as a liturgical and literary language. Today around 9 million people speak Modern Hebrew natively in Israel, where it's the primary official language.

hi.description: An Indo-Aryan language written in the Devanagari script, spoken natively by around 600 million people and serving as one of the two official languages of India's Union government. In its informal spoken form it is mutually intelligible with Urdu, forming the vast 'Hindustani' dialect continuum spoken across northern India and Pakistan.

hr.description: Mutually intelligible South Slavic languages forming a dialect continuum, spoken together by around 21 million people across Croatia, Serbia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, and Montenegro. The main distinction between Croatian and Serbian lies in script (Latin vs. Cyrillic), regional vocabulary, and cultural identity rather than in fundamental grammar.

ht.description: A French-based creole language spoken by virtually all 10–12 million Haitians as their mother tongue, making it the most widely spoken creole language in the world. It emerged from the creative blending of French with West African languages during Haiti's colonial era and gained official status alongside French in 1987.

hu.description: A Uralic language completely unrelated to its Indo-European neighbors in Central Europe, spoken by around 13 million people in Hungary and minority communities in Romania, Slovakia, and Serbia. Notable for its vowel harmony, 18 grammatical cases, complex verb conjugation for object definiteness, and near-total absence of grammatical gender.

hy.description: A unique Indo-European language forming its own branch, written in the distinctive Armenian alphabet created in 405 AD — one of the world's oldest alphabets still in use. Spoken by around 6.7 million people in Armenia and large diaspora communities in Russia, France, and the United States.

id.description: A standardized form of Malay adopted as the official language of Indonesia, the world's fourth most populous country, with around 43 million native speakers and over 200 million who use it as their lingua franca. Its simple grammar — no grammatical genders, no verb tenses, no subject-verb agreement — makes it one of the most accessible major languages.

is.description: A North Germanic language spoken by around 370,000 people in Iceland, so conservative in its evolution that Icelanders can read 13th-century Viking sagas in nearly their original form. Its language council actively coins new vocabulary from Old Norse roots — for example 'tölva' (computer) from 'tala' (number) + 'völva' (seeress).

it.description: A Romance language spoken natively by around 64 million people in Italy, San Marino, Vatican City, Switzerland, and enclaves in Croatia and Slovenia. Often considered the direct descendant of Latin most recognizable to classical scholars, Italian is the language of opera, Renaissance art, Dante, and one of the world's great culinary traditions.

ja.description: A Japonic language spoken natively by around 125 million people, almost exclusively in Japan. Its writing system uniquely combines three scripts — the syllabic hiragana and katakana alphabets alongside thousands of Chinese-derived kanji — and its elaborate honorific register system (keigo) mirrors Japan's intricate social hierarchies.

jv.description: An Austronesian language spoken natively by around 82 million people on the island of Java in Indonesia, making it the most widely spoken regional language in Southeast Asia. Its elaborate speech-level system (ngoko, madya, krama) encodes traditional Javanese social hierarchy into every conversation.

ka.description: A Kartvelian language and the official language of Georgia, written in the elegant, distinctive Georgian script (Mkhedruli) that dates to the 5th century AD. Spoken natively by around 4 million people, it's completely unrelated to any Indo-European language and is typologically remarkable for its complex consonant clusters.

kk.description: A Turkic language spoken natively by around 13–15 million people in Kazakhstan, where it's the state language, and in diaspora communities across Russia and China's Xinjiang region. It has undergone multiple script changes — Arabic to Latin to Cyrillic and now back to Latin — reflecting Kazakhstan's geopolitical shifts across the 20th and 21st centuries.

km.description: The official language of Cambodia, spoken natively by around 16 million people. It uses the Khmer script, which contains more letters than any other writing system in the world (74 letters), and is distinctive among its Southeast Asian neighbors for being non-tonal despite the prevalence of tonal languages in the region.

kn.description: A Dravidian language with a literary tradition spanning over 1,500 years, spoken natively by around 45 million people primarily in the Indian state of Karnataka. It uses its own distinctive Kannada script, one of the oldest surviving scripts in South Asia, and was granted Classical Language status by India in 2008.

ko.description: A language forming its own Koreanic family (with no proven relatives outside a tiny dialect cluster), spoken natively by around 77 million people across South and North Korea and diaspora communities worldwide. Its Hangul alphabet, commissioned by King Sejong the Great in 1443, is celebrated as a triumph of scientific phonological design.

ku.description: An Iranian language spoken natively by around 30–40 million Kurds across Turkey, Iran, Iraq, and Syria — one of the world's largest ethnolinguistic groups without a sovereign state. Its three main dialect groups (Kurmanji, Sorani, and Southern Kurdish) differ enough that they are sometimes treated as separate languages.

ky.description: A Turkic language spoken natively by around 4.5 million people in Kyrgyzstan and neighboring Central Asian countries. Like its Turkic relatives, it features vowel harmony and agglutinative morphology; it was historically written in Arabic and Cyrillic, with recent efforts to introduce a Latin-based alphabet.

lb.description: A Moselle Franconian variety of German elevated to the status of national language in Luxembourg, spoken natively by around 400,000 people. Luxembourg's trilingual reality — Luxembourgish for daily life, French for legislation, and German for administration — makes it a unique European sociolinguistic case study.

lo.description: The official language of Laos, spoken natively by around 7 million people and closely related to Thai, with which it is partially mutually intelligible. Written in a distinctive abugida script, it's a tonal language with 6 tones in the standard Vientiane dialect and is spoken across both banks of the Mekong River.

lt.description: Considered the most archaic of all living Indo-European languages, Lithuanian preserves features of Proto-Indo-European lost in every other branch of the family. Spoken natively by around 3 million people in Lithuania and diaspora communities, it's an indispensable reference point for Indo-European historical linguistics.

lv.description: A Baltic language and one of only two surviving members of the Baltic branch of Indo-European (alongside Lithuanian), spoken natively by around 1.75 million people in Latvia. It retains a distinctive pitch accent system and is invaluable to historical linguists for the archaic Proto-Indo-European features it preserves.

mk.description: A South Slavic language and the official language of North Macedonia, closely related to Bulgarian and Serbian. Spoken by around 2 million people, its written standard was codified only after World War II, and it uses the Cyrillic alphabet in a form specifically tailored to its phonological system.

ml.description: A Dravidian language spoken natively by around 38 million people, primarily in the Indian state of Kerala, which consistently records the highest literacy rates in India. Its script is among the most visually complex in the world — a flowing circular abugida — and it has a rich classical literature tradition.

mn.description: An Altaic-family language spoken natively by around 5.2 million people in Mongolia and Inner Mongolia (China). Traditional Mongolian script — one of the few major scripts that runs vertically from top to bottom — is experiencing a revival in Mongolia alongside the Soviet-era Cyrillic alphabet.

mr.description: An Indo-Aryan language spoken natively by around 83 million people, primarily in the Indian state of Maharashtra. The third-largest language in India by native speakers, it's written in the Devanagari script and has a literary tradition dating to the 13th century, including the devotional poetry of saints like Tukaram and Dnyaneshwar.

ms.description: An Austronesian language and the official language of Malaysia, Brunei, and Singapore (as a national language), spoken natively by around 20 million people. Together with standardized Indonesian, it forms the world's most widely used Austronesian language cluster, understood by over 250 million people across maritime Southeast Asia.

mt.description: The only Semitic language written natively in the Latin alphabet, and one of the official languages of the European Union, spoken by around 520,000 people in Malta. A unique linguistic mosaic, Maltese blends an Arabic-derived base grammar with extensive Sicilian, Italian, English, and French vocabulary.

my.description: The official language of Myanmar, spoken natively by around 33 million people and used as a lingua franca by the country's 54 million inhabitants. It uses a rounded script derived from ancient Mon writing, and its tonal system with complex politeness registers makes it a fascinating typological study.

ne.description: An Indo-Aryan language and the official language of Nepal, also spoken in the Indian state of Sikkim and parts of Bhutan, with around 17 million native speakers. Written in the Devanagari script, it's closely related to Hindi and serves as the lingua franca across Nepal's ethnically diverse Himalayan communities.

nl.description: A West Germanic language spoken natively by around 24 million people in the Netherlands, Belgium (Flanders), Suriname, and the Dutch Caribbean islands. The closest major relative of both German and English, Dutch formed the basis of Afrikaans and once served as a global colonial lingua franca.

no.description: A North Germanic language with two competing official written standards — Bokmål (dominant in cities) and Nynorsk (reviving rural forms) — spoken by around 5.3 million people in Norway. Sitting in the center of the Scandinavian dialect continuum, Norwegian is mutually intelligible with both Danish and Swedish.

oc.description: Once the prestige literary language of medieval Europe — the tongue of the troubadours whose poetry shaped the entire Western lyric tradition — Occitan is now spoken by an estimated 200,000–1.5 million active users across southern France, Monaco, Italy's Occitan Valleys, and Catalonia. Despite centuries of decline, it's experiencing a cultural renaissance through regional media and schools.

pa.description: An Indo-Aryan language spoken natively by around 113 million people, making it one of the world's ten most spoken languages by native speakers. Split between India (where it's written in Gurmukhi script and is the sacred language of Sikhism) and Pakistan (written in Arabic-derived Shahmukhi), its heartland is the fertile Punjab region.

pl.description: A West Slavic language spoken natively by around 45 million people in Poland and large diaspora communities in the USA, UK, and Germany, making it the most spoken Slavic language outside of Russian. Famous for its complex consonant clusters (szcz, źdź, trz), 7 grammatical cases, and being the official language of a major EU economy.

ps.description: An Eastern Iranian language and one of the two official languages of Afghanistan, spoken natively by around 40–60 million people across Afghanistan and northwestern Pakistan. Written in a modified Perso-Arabic script with additional letters for Pashto-specific sounds, it's the mother tongue of the Pashtun people.

pt.description: A Romance language spoken natively by around 250 million people — the sixth-most spoken language in the world by native speakers. Portugal's 15th–16th century empire spread it across Brazil, Angola, Mozambique, Cape Verde, São Tomé, Guinea-Bissau, and East Timor, creating a rich global tapestry of regional varieties.

qu.description: The most widely spoken indigenous language family of the Americas, with around 8–10 million speakers across Peru, Bolivia, Ecuador, Colombia, and Argentina. Once the administrative language of the vast Inca Empire, Quechua's many regional varieties form a dialect continuum, and in Peru and Bolivia it holds co-official status.

ro.description: A Romance language spoken natively by around 24 million people in Romania and Moldova, unique among major Romance languages for retaining a full grammatical case system. As the easternmost large Romance language, Romanian preserves many Latin features lost in its western relatives and has a fascinating layer of Slavic loanwords.

ru.description: An East Slavic language spoken natively by around 150 million people and used as a second language across much of the former Soviet Union, making it the most geographically widespread language in Eurasia. One of the six official languages of the United Nations, Russian has a rich literary tradition including Tolstoy, Dostoevsky, and Chekhov.

sc.description: A Romance language spoken by around 5 million people in Sicily and in diaspora communities worldwide, classified by many linguists as a distinct language rather than a dialect of Italian. It carries layers of Arabic, Norman French, Greek, and Spanish influence, reflecting Sicily's rich history as a crossroads of Mediterranean civilizations.

se.description: The largest of the Sami languages, spoken by around 20,000–30,000 people across the Sápmi region spanning northern Norway, Sweden, and Finland. A Finno-Ugric language with 9 grammatical cases and complex consonant gradation, it's the traditional language of the Sami people — Europe's northernmost indigenous group.

si.description: An Indo-Aryan language spoken natively by around 16 million Sinhalese in Sri Lanka, where it's an official language alongside Tamil. Written in the ornate, circular Sinhala script, it features a striking diglossia — formal written Sinhala and everyday colloquial speech differ so significantly that they are sometimes treated as separate registers.

sk.description: A West Slavic language closely related to Czech, spoken natively by around 5 million people in Slovakia. While highly mutually intelligible with Czech, Slovak has its own phonological system, vocabulary, and 6-case grammar, and the two languages diverged significantly during centuries of separate political histories.

sl.description: A South Slavic language spoken natively by around 2.5 million people in Slovenia, remarkable for preserving the grammatical dual number — a distinct form for referring to exactly two of something — lost in most other Slavic languages. Its 46 recognized dialects show extraordinary internal variation for such a small language community.

so.description: A Cushitic language spoken natively by around 21 million Somalis across Somalia, Djibouti, Ethiopia, and Kenya, with diaspora communities across Europe and North America. A written Somali standard using the Latin alphabet was only established in 1972; before that, the language had a rich oral tradition of poetry considered a national art form.

sq.description: An Indo-European language forming its own branch with no close living relatives, spoken natively by around 7.5 million Albanians across Albania, Kosovo, North Macedonia, and diaspora communities worldwide. Its two main dialects — Gheg in the north and Tosk in the south — differ significantly in phonology and vocabulary.

srd.description: Often described as the most conservative of all Romance languages, Sardinian preserves phonological and grammatical features from Latin that have been lost in every other Romance language — making it a living linguistic time capsule. Spoken by around 1–1.3 million people in Sardinia, it has official regional recognition in Italy.

sv.description: A North Germanic language spoken natively by around 10–13 million people in Sweden and Finland, and the most widely spoken of the Scandinavian languages by native count. Its characteristic singsong pitch accent (two tones), mutually intelligibility with Norwegian and Danish, and Sweden's significant cultural exports make it a high-value learning target.

sw.description: A Bantu language serving as the primary lingua franca across East and Central Africa, with around 200 million total speakers. Official in Tanzania, Kenya, Uganda, the DRC, and the African Union itself, Swahili is the most studied African language in the world and is notable for its relatively simple agglutinative grammar.

ta.description: A Dravidian language with one of the world's longest unbroken literary traditions, with Tamil texts dated to over 2,000 years ago. Spoken natively by around 75–80 million people in Tamil Nadu, Sri Lanka, Singapore, and diaspora communities, Tamil is one of the world's few classical languages that is also a thriving, evolving mother tongue.

te.description: A Dravidian language spoken natively by around 83 million people in the Indian states of Andhra Pradesh and Telangana, often called 'the Italian of the East' by linguists for its melodic, vowel-ending words. Telugu has a classical literature tradition exceeding 1,000 years and was designated a Classical Language of India in 2008.

tg.description: An Iranian language very closely related to Persian and Dari, serving as the official language of Tajikistan with around 8–9 million native speakers. Unlike its Persian and Afghan relatives, Tajik is written in the Cyrillic alphabet — a legacy of Soviet policy — though efforts to restore the Persian script are ongoing.

th.description: A Kra-Dai language and the official language of Thailand, spoken natively by around 70 million people. A tonal language with 5 tones written in its own abugida script (44 consonants, 15 vowel symbols), Thai has an intricate system of honorific vocabulary (Rachasap) reserved for speaking to or about the monarchy.

ti.description: A Semitic language spoken natively by around 9–10 million people in Eritrea and the Tigray region of Ethiopia, written in the ancient Ethiopic (Ge'ez) script. It's the most widely spoken language in Eritrea and one of the country's official working languages, with a tradition of liturgical use in the Ethiopian Orthodox Church.

tk.description: A Turkic language spoken natively by around 5–7 million people in Turkmenistan and minority communities in Afghanistan and Iran. Sharing significant mutual intelligibility with Turkish and Uzbek, it was written in Arabic, then Latin, then Cyrillic during the Soviet era, and switched back to a Latin-based alphabet in 1993.

tl.description: An Austronesian language and the basis of Filipino, the national language of the Philippines, with around 28 million native speakers concentrated in Luzon and the Manila capital region. Its standardized form (Filipino) draws on vocabulary from English, Spanish, and other Philippine languages and is understood across the nation's 110+ million people.

tr.description: A Turkic language spoken natively by around 80 million people in Turkey and Cyprus, known for its highly agglutinative structure where entire sentences can be expressed as single words through suffix chains. Atatürk's 1928 script reform replaced the Arabic alphabet with a Latin-based one, making Turkish one of the most accessible Turkic languages for learners.

tt.description: A Turkic language spoken natively by around 5–6 million Tatars, primarily in Russia's Republic of Tatarstan and Bashkortostan. Closely related to Bashkir, it uses the Cyrillic alphabet in Russia, though efforts to restore the Latin script used before Stalinist repression are ongoing.

ug.description: A Turkic language spoken natively by around 12 million Uyghurs in China's Xinjiang region and diaspora communities across Central Asia and Kazakhstan. Written in the Arabic script (reading right to left), it has a rich classical literary tradition under the Chagatai language and is closely related to Uzbek.

uk.description: An East Slavic language spoken natively by around 40 million people in Ukraine, most closely related to Belarusian and sharing significant vocabulary with Russian while being a fully distinct language. Written in Cyrillic in a distinct orthography, Ukrainian's identity as a separate language — once suppressed — has become a profound symbol of national resilience.

ur.description: An Indo-Aryan language and the national language of Pakistan, spoken natively by around 70–80 million people and understood across much of South Asia. Written in the elegant Nastaliq calligraphic style of the Arabic script (right to left), it's largely mutually intelligible with Hindi in spoken form but diverges sharply in formal vocabulary.

uz.description: A Turkic language spoken natively by around 35 million people, making it the most widely spoken Turkic language in Central Asia. Uzbekistan switched from Cyrillic to a Latin-based alphabet in 1993, and Uzbek serves as the official language across a strategically important country at the heart of the ancient Silk Road.

vi.description: An Austroasiatic language spoken natively by around 77 million people in Vietnam. Distinctively written in Chữ Quốc Ngữ — a Latin-based alphabet developed by Jesuit missionaries, using diacritical marks to encode its six tones — Vietnamese is an isolating, analytical language despite its geographic proximity to more morphologically complex neighbors.

yi.description: A High German-derived language written in the Hebrew alphabet, historically the vernacular of Ashkenazi Jewish communities across Eastern Europe with a peak of around 11–13 million speakers before the Holocaust. Today around 1–1.5 million speakers maintain living Yiddish, primarily in ultra-Orthodox communities in Israel, New York, and Antwerp.

yo.description: A Niger-Congo language spoken natively by around 45 million people primarily in southwestern Nigeria, Benin, and Togo. One of Africa's most documented and internationally taught indigenous languages, Yoruba has a three-tone tonal system, a rich oral tradition, and the Ifá divination corpus recognized by UNESCO as an Intangible Cultural Heritage.

yue.description: A Sinitic language spoken natively by around 85 million people in Guangdong province, Hong Kong, and Macau, and is the dominant language of Chinese diaspora communities worldwide. While sharing the Chinese writing system with Mandarin, spoken Cantonese is mutually unintelligible with it and preserves many Middle Chinese features lost in other varieties.

zh.description: The most widely spoken language by native speakers in the world, with around 920 million native speakers across China, Taiwan, and Southeast Asia. A tonal language with four tones plus a neutral tone, it uses thousands of logographic characters rather than an alphabet, and Mandarin Chinese serves as the standard spoken form (Putonghua) across the diverse Sinophone world.

zu.description: A Bantu language and the most widely spoken indigenous language of South Africa, with around 12–14 million native speakers. Zulu is notable for its click consonants (c, q, x) borrowed from neighboring Khoisan languages, its vibrant Zulu music scene (isicathamiya, maskandi), and its role as one of South Africa's 11 official languages.

lsg_glossary.fusional: A morphological type where a single suffix bundles several meanings (number, case, gender at once). Latin and Russian are fusional.
lsg_glossary.agglutinative: A morphological type where each meaning is expressed by its own clearly separable suffix, stacked in sequence. Turkish and Finnish are agglutinative.
lsg_glossary.analytic: A morphological type that relies on separate words and word order rather than inflection. Chinese and Vietnamese are highly analytic.
lsg_glossary.V2: Verb-second word order — the finite verb always lands in the second position of a main clause regardless of what comes first. German and Dutch are V2.
lsg_glossary.SOV: Subject-Object-Verb word order. Japanese, Korean, Turkish, and Hindi are SOV.
lsg_glossary.SVO: Subject-Verb-Object word order. English, Spanish, and Mandarin are SVO.
lsg_glossary.vowel harmony: A constraint where vowels within a word must share certain features (e.g. all front or all back). Common in Turkic, Uralic, and Mongolic.
lsg_glossary.pitch accent: A system where the meaningful prominence on a syllable is realised as a pitch movement rather than a stress, used in Japanese and Swedish.
lsg_glossary.tone: When pitch contour distinguishes word meaning (Mandarin mā/má/mǎ/mà = mother/hemp/horse/scold). Common in Sino-Tibetan and Niger-Congo.
lsg_glossary.cognate: A word in two languages that descends from the same ancestor word, e.g. English "night" and Spanish "noche" both from Latin nox.
lsg_glossary.loanword: A word borrowed from another language during contact, not inherited. "Sushi" in English is a loan from Japanese.
lsg_glossary.sprachbund: A group of geographically adjacent but unrelated languages that share structural features through long contact (e.g. the Balkan sprachbund).
lsg_glossary.sub-branch: A finer subdivision below a branch. West Germanic is a sub-branch of the Germanic branch.
lsg_glossary.branch: A first-level subdivision of a language family. Germanic, Romance, Slavic are branches of Indo-European.
lsg_glossary.family: The largest grouping of demonstrably related languages, sharing a common ancestor (proto-language).
lsg_glossary.phoneme: A meaningfully distinct sound in a language. English /p/ and /b/ are different phonemes because they distinguish "pat" from "bat".
lsg_glossary.morphology: The system of word internal structure — how words are built from smaller meaningful pieces (roots, affixes, etc.).
lsg_glossary.orthography: The writing system and spelling conventions used to represent a language.
lsg_glossary.lexical similarity: How much of two languages’ core vocabularies look the same — usually measured by counting shared cognates in basic word-lists.
lsg_glossary.genealogical distance: How far back in time the most recent common ancestor of two languages lived; measured by branching depth in the family tree.
lsg_glossary.Latin script: The writing system used by English and most of Western Europe; descended from Roman alphabets.
lsg_glossary.Cyrillic script: The writing system used by Russian and most Slavic Orthodox-tradition languages; descended from Greek.
lsg_glossary.creole: A stable contact language that emerged from a pidgin, with a fully developed grammar of its own. Haitian Creole and Tok Pisin are creoles.
lsg_glossary.isolate: A language with no known living relatives. Basque, Burushaski, and Korean (debated) are isolates.
